From Prompt Rules to Golden Data Model: Production-Scale Generation of Personalized, Compliant Pharmaceutical Claims

Suyash Mishra Affiliation: Roche Email: mailto:upender.phogat@involead.comupender.phogat@involead.com    Qiang Li Affiliation: Accenture Email: mailto:srikanth.patil@involead.comsrikanth.patil@involead.com    Subhabrata Adak Affiliation: Involead Correspondence:suyash.mishra@roche.com, qiang.i.li@accenture.com, subhabrata.adak@involead.com Email: mailto:satyanarayan.pati@involead.comsatyanarayan.pati@involead.com    Upender Phogat Affiliation: Involead Correspondence:suyash.mishra@roche.com, qiang.i.li@accenture.com, subhabrata.adak@involead.com    Srikanth Patil Affiliation: Involead Correspondence:suyash.mishra@roche.com, qiang.i.li@accenture.com, subhabrata.adak@involead.com    Satyanarayan Pati Affiliation: Involead Correspondence:suyash.mishra@roche.com, qiang.i.li@accenture.com, subhabrata.adak@involead.com
Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate domain-specific commercial & medical content (e.g., claims, statements, and promotional phrases) in regulated industries such as pharmaceuticals. However, ensuring its regulatory compliance, factual accuracy, and audience-specific personalization remains a major challenge. We report a production case study asking whether moving compliance and personalization signal from prompt-level rules into retrieval-time structured context improves pharmaceutical claims generation, using Composer, a deployed internal tool built on a Golden Data Model (GDM) of 1,867 pharmaceutical claims spanning four products. The GDM integrates claim metadata, references, audience labels, material type, usage history, Match Text Variant (MTV) links, and a six-dimension quality score (6C). Across six product-audience segments, the context pipeline improves intended indication (+29%), intended content type (+62%) and intended target audience (+67%), 6C quality score (+86%), and claim reuse (+34%). Production log analysis over the deployment period shows a 29.5% reduction in weekly API cost. We report this as descriptive deployment evidence. This work is a systems and data-architecture contribution: it shows that in a regulated, high-stakes domain, restructuring claim data for retrieval-time filtering is a more scalable lever than expanding prompt-level rules, and documents the engineering path data cleaning, graph linking, and quality scoring Check our Composer Video.

1 Introduction

AI-generated text has been detected increasingly in medical literature Wolfrath et al. (2026). A 2025 market forecast projected the AI in medical writing market to reach USD 1,760.02 million by 2030, with a CAGR of 12.52% from 2025 to 2030 Grand View Research (2025). However, their deployment in regulated domains such as healthcare and pharmaceuticals remains constrained by persistent concerns around hallucination, regulatory compliance, and limited controllability Hager et al. (2024).

Pharmacy content generation is particularly challenging. Claims must be: (i) factually grounded in approved sources, (ii) compliant with regulatory constraints, (iii) tailored to specific audiences such as healthcare professionals (HCPs) or patients  Barrias et al. (2024).

Our baseline relies on rule-based prompting and strict templates. In our deployment, this baseline often failed to produce personalized and contextually appropriate outputs. As observed in real-world systems, rule-based approaches can lead to mismatches in target audience, low relevance, and overuse of inactive or general claims.

In contrast, context-rich approaches leverage structured data, usage history, and semantic relationships to guide generation. However, the effectiveness of such approaches has not been experimentally studied. In this paper, we address following core research question:

Does shifting compliance and personalization signals from prompt-level rules to structured retrieval-time data improve the quality and production efficiency of pharmaceutical claim generation in a deployed system?

To answer this, we propose a golden data model schema that transforms fragmented claim data into a structured, graph-based representation with quality-aware filtering. We further evaluate rule-based and context-based generation pipelines across multiple dimensions, including compliance (e.g., prohibited words / phrases, target indication / type, MTV-Variant claims reuse), personalization (e.g. target audience), and quality (6C scores). We note that the context pipeline does not eliminate rules outright, claim-level guardrails and prohibited-word constraints still persist, but relocates them from static, product-level prompt text to claim-level, retrieval-gated metadata.

2 Related Work

Pharmaceutical content management: Veeva PromoMats supports promotional content and claims management, including substantiation and contextual claim variations Veeva Systems (n.d.). IQVIA provides HCP engagement solutions IQVIA (n.d.). These product descriptions do not establish the internal generation architectures of the platforms. Our contribution is a production evaluation of an explicit claim-centered schema and audience-conditioned generation pipeline. Prior research has examined the informational and emotional content of prescription-drug advertising Frosch et al. (2007) and the distinction between promotion and scientific exchange Kessler (1991).

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in biomedical NLP: RAG  Gao et al. (2023); Asai et al. (2024) improves grounding by incorporating external knowledge sources. RAG has improved factuality in knowledge-intensive generation Lewis et al. (2020), whereas chain-of-thought prompting has improved arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning Wei et al. (2022); the latter does not by itself establish reduced hallucination. However, standard RAG systems lack domain-specific constraints such as regulatory compliance and structured claim validation. RAG alone is insufficient for pharmaceutical claim generation because it does not enforce the audience-specific stylistic transformation that distinguishes a KOL-facing mechanism statement from a patient-facing aspirational statement derived from the same input. Prior work in biomedical NLP, has mostly focused on information extraction and summarization, but less attention has been given to controlled, personalized generation under strict regulatory requirements. Our work differs in two key aspects: (1) we introduce a data-centric framework for controlling generation, and (2) we provide an empirical comparison between rule-based and context-based approaches in real-world setting.

Verification and hallucination evaluation: Recent benchmarks such as SciVer (Wang et al., 2025) evaluate multimodal scientific claim verification with expert-annotated supporting evidence. HonestVQA (Tripathi et al., 2025) studies confidence calibration in document visual question answering, while Decomposed NLI (DNLI) (Yanuka et al., 2025) evaluates individual propositions in image captions. MLLMGuard (Gu et al., 2024) assesses multimodal safety across privacy, bias, toxicity, truthfulness, and legality. Industrial traffic-incident benchmarks also examine LLM hallucination (Li et al., 2025). These studies concern distinct tasks and do not directly validate pharmaceutical claim generation.

3 Methodology

Given a target audience (e.g., HCP, Patient), content type (e.g., Email, Banner), and a set of claims, the goal is to generate compliant and personalized text. The rule-based approach relies on predefined instructions, including: strict citation rules, verbatim claim usage constraints, and template-based generation. While this ensures high compliance, it limits flexibility and personalization. We propose a golden data model schema that enhances claim usability via 4 key components as shown in Fig 2:

1. Semantic Integrity Layer: periodic pipeline executing high-volume "upserts" from Veeva Vault and other sources into the central library. Claims are clustered using keywords and embeddings to identify duplicates, near-duplicates, contradictions.

2. Graph-Based Representation: Claims are linked to: references, materials, audience metadata, forming a relational graph structure (as shown in Appendix Figure 6. This is the relationship building layer. Establishes the structural links between Claims, References, and Materials. It aggregates metadata to provide a unified view of derivation and utilization, stored in Graph DB.

3. 6C Quality Framework: Each claim is then scored along six dimensions: Clarity, Completeness, Consistency, Connectivity, Compliance, Context, as shown in Table 10 how weights differ, Table 11 why each dimension is scored this way, Table 12 what it evaluates. It translates relational evidence into a mathematical "Strength Score", quantifies how firmly a claim to its supporting scientific text.

4. Alignment Annotation Protocol. Indication, content-type, and target audience alignment were then judged by internal US medical-content writers team not involved in system development, using binary match against the campaign brief’s stated indication/content-type/ audience fields. Judgment was BLINDED to pipeline (Pre vs. Post).

5. Audience Lens: Claims are filtered and ranked based on target audience, region, and usage patterns. This is the reconciliation action layer - the final decision gate. Based on 6C scores, status, and recency, it executes the "Golden Actions" (Merge/Suppress/Flag), publishing the final, high-integrity records to the Gold Layer Graph DB.

In our context-based approach, the LLM then retrieves top-ranked claims, applies semantic filtering and ranking, generates outputs conditioned on high-quality, audience-specific claims.

4 Dataset and Experimental Settings

We construct our dataset of more than 1,800 pharmaceutical claims across 4 products: Hemlibra, Ocrevus, Ocrevus Zunovo, and Vabysmo. The claims span 11 categories, including disease education, efficacy, safety, dosing and administration, clinical practice guidelines, and patient access. All claims are retrieved from Veeva and are associated with metadata such as references, usage history, and audience annotations. We evaluate the two pipelines using Claude Sonnet 4.5, the production model for Composer; we additionally report per-token cost benchmarks for Gemini 2.5 Pro/Flash, the deployment comparison in §5 uses Sonnet 4.5 throughout  Google Cloud (n.d.); Anthropic (2025b) across multi-dimensions: 1. Compliance Rate & Claim Utilization: The percentage of outputs that correctly use approved claims, the proportion of relevant claims used, and content-type alignment with intended format. 2. Personalization Accuracy & 6C Score: Alignment with target audience and the average quality of selected claims measured by 6C scoring (A.2). 3. Deployment API Cost & Latency: Request-level scalability metrics, including success rate, average latency, P50 latency, request tokens per week, total cost, and tokens per request.

5 Main Results

Our results show that context-based generation outperforms rule-based pipeline, Fig. 7 Pre-pipeline legacy rule diagram.

Compliance & Personalization: Context-based generation achieves near-perfect compliance across all segments, compared to lower compliance in rule-based setups. In the existing Pre-setup "rule-based pipeline" only 71% of the claims are aligned with the intended indication, only 38% of the claims are aligned with the intended content type, only 33% of the claims are aligned with the intended target audience. However, as shown Table 3, post context pipeline 100% claims are matching with intended indication, intended content type and intended target audience. Furthermore, examining Table 6 shows that this improvement generalizes across product level, specifically for Vabysmo and Ocrevus, as well as across role types, including HCPs, nurses, and patients’ physicians.

We distinguish two classes of metric in this evaluation. Structurally guaranteed metrics — indication, content-type, and target-audience alignment, and "approved claims used" — are enforced by the Post pipeline’s retrieval filters by construction: Composer only retrieves claims that already match the requested indication/content-type/audience, so 100% alignment on these dimensions reflects the filter design. We report them because the Pre pipeline’s failure to enforce the same constraints (33–71%). Learned or judged metrics — MTV utilization, 6C quality score of selected claims are not guaranteed by construction and are the metrics that actually test whether structured context improves outcomes.

Alignment with target audience rate improves substantially, with context-based pipeline, the content generation (Post) achieved 100% compliance with approved claims, compared to 71% in previously created content.

Claim Utilization: as shown in Table 2 and Table 13, the use of high-quality claims increases, particularly for previously underutilized claim variants. Raw claim repositories are structurally rich but operationally underutilized without contextual modeling, e.g., Ocrevus: 31.65% MTV (Variants of Claim) exists but only 8.68% used. High claims coverage but low MTV usage with avg only 17.68%. Vabysmo leads in MTV coverage (55.68%) with relatively higher linkage, Hemlibra has the highest absolute MTV usage (187 used in materials), Ocrevus & Ocrevus Zunovo show low utilization, indicating a higher reliance on direct claim text instead of MTVs (Only 6.56 % - 8.68%). Overall, MTV availability is 42.69%, while only 17.68% are utilized in materials, highlighting a significant usage gap. Further shown in Table 3, after the context pipeline, the MTV claim utilization increased 34%, unlocking previously unused claim across all segments (see Table 6: MTV).

Quality & 6C:

As shown in Table 5, the Average 6C scores are higher in the context-based approach, indicating improved clarity, consistency, and contextual relevance. POST dominates PRE in almost all segments, especially: VAB DMe Patient: 0.0 →\rightarrow 0.86, OCR MS Nurse: 0.83 →\rightarrow 0.91, VAB-DME-Patient: 0 re-used claims to all re-used claims. This is clear evidence our golden data model improves quality. With the higher-scoring 6C claims are used in content generation, we also see the cost reduced, as shown in left side Table 4, the deployed context pipeline substantially reduces response-token generation by 65.4%, suggesting cleaner and more controlled outputs. It also improves the request success rate from 99.2% to 100%. In practice, the total cost is not determined only by the cost of a single generation call, but also by user behavior and re-generation frequency. When generated outputs are better aligned with the user’s intent, target audience, and content constraints, users may need fewer repeated requests to obtain satisfactory results. Therefore, the cost profile is not a simple binary outcome. If the context pipeline were used at the same request volume as Pre, the total cost would increase by roughly 35%, consistent with the higher average cost per request. In the observed deployment, however, the number of requests decreased from 5,485 to 2,871, resulting in a lower total weekly cost.

In addition, with Figure 5 and Appendix Table 11, it is suggested that rule-based constraints alone are insufficient for complex generation tasks. While they enforce correctness, they fail to capture contextual nuances required for personalization. In contrast, structured contextual data enables the model to select more relevant claims, adapt to audience-specific needs, and maintain compliance via data filtering rather than prompt constraints. This also highlights the importance of data-centric approaches in controlling LLM behavior.

6 Conclusion

This work demonstrates that structured context moving compliance and personalization signal from prompt-level rules into retrieval-time claim metadata provides a more scalable and effective architecture for content generation in a regulated industry than expanding prompt-level rules alone. We evaluated across compliance, target-audience, indication, content-type alignment, MTV reuse, latency, token usage, request success rate, and API cost. We also formalized 6C Algorithm for evaluating claim quality across Clarity, Completeness, Consistency, Connectivity, Compliance, and Context Availability. Our results show that the context-based pipeline improves compliance while reducing total weekly cost. Although richer retrieval increases the average cost per request, the overall system becomes more efficient - cleaner outputs, and a higher success rate. This work demonstrates that structured context rather than explicit rule instructions provides a more effective LLM solution for regulated industry.

7 Limitations and Ethic Statements

This study focuses on a real-world pharmaceutical content generation setting, where regulatory compliance, claim traceability, and audience-specific adaptation are central requirements. The dataset reflects approved claim assets from selected pharmaceutical products and specific market context, which enables detailed analysis of compliance-sensitive generation. Due to the regulated and proprietary nature of the underlying claim data, we cannot release the full production dataset. To support transparency and reproducibility, we also provide representative cleaned examples, schema-level records, scoring rubrics, and system-level descriptions, logs, tool videos in the appendix. The observed efficiency gains are based on production log analysis. These results should therefore be interpreted as deployment-level evidence rather than a purely model-intrinsic efficiency claim.

Our current experiments focus on pharmaceutical compliance because it represents a high-stakes domain where controllable and evidence-grounded generation is especially important. Future work will extend the proposed data-centric approach to additional regulated domains, such as financial services and manufacturing, to further assess its generalizability across different compliance and content-governance settings.

Composer generates promotional and medical content for real pharmaceutical products.All generated content passes through existing MLR (Medical, Legal, Regulatory) review before reaching end users; Composer does not publish directly to patients or HCPs. LLM-derived guardrails and prohibited-phrase constraints (Table 1) are validated and derived from and cross-checked against the original approved claim text at generation time, with human review flagged in the schema. Provenance and approval status are preserved through canonicalization process when records are reconciled in the Golden Layer.

A.1 Ablation study: framework perform in terms of token count, latency, and monetary cost

In addition, we record per-request token usage and billing of production logs from different model providers. Gemini 2.5 Flash requests cost sub-cent (e.g.,  0.38–0.64¢ for  1.8–1.9K tokens), while Gemini 2.5 Pro typically costs a few cents per request. For Anthropic endpoints, observed costs were also low (e.g.,  1.46–3.93¢ for  4–11.9K tokens;  0.32–0.37¢ per 1K tokens), which enables scalability for industry application.

The model used in Table  4 both settings is us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5. The cost comparison reveals an interesting trade-off. After integrating the context pipeline, The observed weekly API cost fell from 128.70​t​o128.70to90.69 (−-29.5%) across the measurement window, driven by a drop in request volume (5,485 →\rightarrow 2,871) that outweighs the 35% higher average cost per request. We hypothesize this reflects fewer re-generation requests as output quality improves, consistent with the 65.4% drop in response-token generation. Here we did not measure regeneration rate, active-user counts, or campaign mix directly. We therefore report this as descriptive deployment evidence of an association between the context pipeline and lower weekly spend.

However, the deployed context pipeline substantially reduces response-token generation by 65.4%. It also improves the request success rate from 99.2% to 100%. In practice, the total cost is not determined only by the cost of a single generation call, but also by user behavior and re-generation frequency. When generated outputs are better aligned with the user’s intent, target audience, and content constraints, users may need fewer repeated requests to obtain satisfactory results.

Therefore, the cost profile is not a simple binary outcome. This suggests that business-level efficiency depends jointly on API cost per request, request volume, success rate, and perceived output quality.

A.2 Ablation study: the 6C Scoring Framework

The 6C Scoring Framework evaluates claims across six dimensions (the "6 C’s"). Each dimension scores between 0.0 and 1.0. Connectivity is evaluated first based on the presence of references, materials, and archived references. Compliance is evaluated next, it requires that connectivity has passed (score >= 0.9) and checks life-cycle approval status. Context Availability is evaluated only after both connectivity and compliance have been established. Clarity, Completeness, and Consistency are evaluated in parallel via LLM calls.

The scoring pipeline follows these steps:

  • •

    Data retrieval: Claims and MTV (Match Text Variant) data are fetched from the Neo4j graph database  Robinson et al. (2015) along with their linked References and Materials.

  • •

    Connectivity scoring: Each claim is scored based on the presence of its linked references, archived references, and materials.

  • •

    Compliance scoring: Claims that pass connectivity are checked for life-cycle approval status.

  • •

    Parallel LLM evaluation: Three concurrent API calls to Claude Sonnet 4 evaluate Clarity, Completeness, and Consistency. LLM-based assessment is motivated by prior evaluation studies Zheng et al. (2023); Liu et al. (2023); Claude Sonnet 4 is documented separately Anthropic (2025a).

  • •

    Context Availability scoring: Computed deterministically from metadata column availability (requires connectivity and compliance first).

  • •

    Final aggregation: The 6C Score is the weighted arithmetic mean of all six dimension scores.

Here, for LLM Configuration Model,we use us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-20250514-v1:0 (AWS Bedrock)  Anthropic (2025a), Temperature we set 0.0 (low-temperature sampling)and Max Tokens: 65,000, Concurrency: 40 parallel evaluations.

For each claim xix_{i}, we compute a six-dimensional quality vector:

𝐬i=[siclar,sicomp,sicons,siconn,sicompl,sictx],\mathbf{s}_{i}=[s_{i}^{\mathrm{clar}},s_{i}^{\mathrm{comp}},s_{i}^{\mathrm{cons}},s_{i}^{\mathrm{conn}},s_{i}^{\mathrm{compl}},s_{i}^{\mathrm{ctx}}],

where each dimension score is bounded in [0,1][0,1]. The final 6C score is a weighted arithmetic mean:

S6​C​(xi)=∑k=16wk​si(k),∑k=16wk=1,si(k)∈[0,1].S_{6C}(x_{i})=\sum_{k=1}^{6}w_{k}s_{i}^{(k)},\quad\sum_{k=1}^{6}w_{k}=1,\quad s_{i}^{(k)}\in[0,1].

In our experiments, we assign equal weights to all six dimensions:

wk=16.w_{k}=\frac{1}{6}.

Thus:

S6​C​(xi)=16​(CLOSE\displaystyle S_{6C}(x_{i})=\frac{1}{6}\Big( siclar+sicomp+sicons\displaystyle s_{i}^{\mathrm{clar}}+s_{i}^{\mathrm{comp}}+s_{i}^{\mathrm{cons}}
OPEN+siconn+sicompl+sictx).\displaystyle+s_{i}^{\mathrm{conn}}+s_{i}^{\mathrm{compl}}+s_{i}^{\mathrm{ctx}}\Big).

Clarity.

Clarity evaluates whether a claim is clearly written and scientifically precise:

siclar\displaystyle s_{i}^{\mathrm{clar}} =0.15​h1+0.15​h2+0.15​h3+0.15​h4\displaystyle=0.15h_{1}+0.15h_{2}+0.15h_{3}+0.15h_{4}
+0.15​h5+0.15​h6+0.10​h7\displaystyle+0.15h_{5}+0.15h_{6}+0.10h_{7}

Inputs: Product, Indication, Claim Text, and Reference Text.

Completeness.

Completeness evaluates whether the claim is structurally whole, self-contained, and legally anchored:

sicomp=0.30​h1+0.25​h2+0.15​h3+0.15​h4+0.15​h5s_{i}^{\mathrm{comp}}=0.30h_{1}+0.25h_{2}+0.15h_{3}+0.15h_{4}+0.15h_{5}

Inputs: Product, Indication, Claim Text, and Reference Text.

Consistency.

Consistency evaluates semantic alignment across the claim text, Match Text Variant, and material text:

sicons=0.35​h1+0.25​h2+0.20​h3+0.20​h4s_{i}^{\mathrm{cons}}=0.35h_{1}+0.25h_{2}+0.20h_{3}+0.20h_{4}

Inputs: Product, Indication, Claim Text, Reference Text, Matched Variation Text, and Material Text.

Let ℳ\mathcal{M} denote the set of required metadata fields:

ℳ\displaystyle\mathcal{M} ={Indication,ScientificArea,PrimaryLocation,\displaystyle=\{\textit{Indication},\textit{ScientificArea},\textit{PrimaryLocation},
ClaimCategory,REFAnchorID,,\displaystyle\text{ClaimCategory},\textit{REFAnchorID},,
MaterialLinkedText,\displaystyle\textit{MaterialLinkedText},
TargetAudience,ContentType}.\displaystyle\textit{TargetAudience},\textit{ContentType}\}.

For claim xix_{i}, let mim_{i} be the number of missing fields in ℳ\mathcal{M}. The Context Availability score is:

sictx=max⁡(0,1−mi|ℳ|)=max⁡(0,1−mi8).s_{i}^{\mathrm{ctx}}=\max\left(0,1-\frac{m_{i}}{|\mathcal{M}|}\right)=\max\left(0,1-\frac{m_{i}}{8}\right).

Dependency structure.

The data-driven dimensions are evaluated with gating dependencies:

siconn=fconn​(ri,ai,mi),s_{i}^{\mathrm{conn}}=f_{\mathrm{conn}}(r_{i},a_{i},m_{i}),

where rir_{i}, aia_{i}, and mim_{i} indicate the availability of active references, archived references, and linked materials.

Compliance is conditioned on connectivity:

sicompl=fcompl​(siconn,ℓi),s_{i}^{\mathrm{compl}}=f_{\mathrm{compl}}(s_{i}^{\mathrm{conn}},\ell_{i}),

where ℓi\ell_{i} denotes the lifecycle state. In our implementation, a claim receives full compliance credit only when:

siconn≥0.9∧ℓi∈{Approved,Approved State}.s_{i}^{\mathrm{conn}}\geq 0.9\quad\land\quad\ell_{i}\in\{\text{Approved},\text{Approved State}\}.

Context availability is evaluated after connectivity and compliance have been established:

sictx=𝕀[siconn≥0.9]⋅𝕀[sicompl>0]⋅max(0,1−mi8).s_{i}^{\mathrm{ctx}}=\mathbb{I}[s_{i}^{\mathrm{conn}}\geq 0.9]\cdot\mathbb{I}[s_{i}^{\mathrm{compl}}>0]\cdot\max\left(0,1-\frac{m_{i}}{8}\right).

A.3 Ablation Study: Post-Deployment Composer Usage Patterns

Problem:Can Composer generate emails and banners that better match the target audience, user intent, indication, and content format while reducing production API costs?

What we did: We compared the original rule-based pipeline with a new context-based pipeline powered by the Golden Data Model. The original pipeline primarily relied on prompt instructions and approved-claim rules. In contrast, the Golden Data Model provides structured claim-level context, including references, audience labels, MTV links, 6C scores, and LLM-derived tags for hallucination prevention and prohibited wording.

Outcome: The logs contain 16,963 requests, 146 million tokens,and an estimated monthly API cost of $543.39. We evaluated model-side measures, including input and output tokens, latency, and success rate, and user-side measures, including daily activity, request volume, and likely regeneration behavior. The results indicate systematic human usage rather than random API traffic. Wednesdays generally show lower activity, whereas Mondays, Tuesdays, and Fridays show higher activity, which helps identify safer windows for system updates and support planning. Our context-based pipeline also required fewer repeated requests and increased the target-audience match rate by 67%.
